passages.quote:
uments can include:

your passport or other identity documents

qualification certificates and transcripts

evidence of professional registration or membership in the UK (if applicable)

references, employment history, or evidence of practice hours

evidence of professional indemnity insurance (for some professions)

criminal record or fitness to practise checks (for some professions)

certified translations, if required

Common requirements and things to prepare for

Countries with state, provincial or territorial regulation

If regulation is set at state, provincial or territorial level, you may need to repeat steps 1 to 4 for the specific jurisdiction where you will work. Ask whether the regulator recognises your qualification for that jurisdiction, and whether you can transfer recognition if you later move within the country.

Fees and timescales

Costs and processing times vary widely. As well as application fees, you may need to budget for translations, certification of documents, travel, and any tests or courses required by the regulator.

Language requirements

Some regulators require evidence of language proficiency, especially where you will have direct contact with the public. Requirements can include formal tests or evidence of professional experience in the language.

Tests, interviews or supervised practice

If the regulator identifies differences between your UK qualification and the local requirements, you may need to do one of the following:

take an aptitude test

complete an interview

complete an online learning module

undertake a period of supervised practice or adaptation

Translating and certifying documents

You may need to provide certified copies and certified translations of your documents. Some countries also require documents to be authenticated (for example, using an apostille). Check the regulator’s guidance before you pay for translations or certification.

If you cannot get recognition

If you cannot get your qualification recognised, or the process would take too long, you may have other options depending on your profession and target market.

For example:

ask the regulator whether there are alternative routes (such as, an assessment based on professional experience)

consider roles where recognition is not required, or where you work under supervision

consider completing any additional training, tests or local qualifications needed

ask the regulator about review or appeal processes if your application is refused

Get help and related guidance

Start with the overseas regulator or competent authority for your profession, as they can tell you the correct route and requirements.

Use the UK Regulated Professions Register to check whether your profession is regulated in the UK and who the UK regulator is.

If you are providing professional services overseas (for example, as a self-employed professional or through your employer), business.gov.uk has export support guidance on recognition of professional qualifications and how to get help from the export support team.

For background on recognition arrangements, read ‘Arrangements to facilitate the recognition of professional qualifications’.

If you are providing services in the EU, read ‘Recognition of UK professional qualifications in EU member states’.

This guidance provides general information. If you spot something that is out of date, choose the ‘Report a problem with this page’ button at the end of this GOV.UK webpage.

Annex 1: a select list of arrangements that UK regulated sectors have with international partners

Wording index

The following are descriptions of types of agreements but titling may vary in the agreements themselves.

Bilateral accreditation arrangement

This provides recognition of qualifications from specific accredited education providers or programmes, rather than reciprocal recognition between regulatory bodies.

Direct Membership Agreement (one way)

This provides a one-way membership route for eligible members. Local practising rights are not automatically conferred and local licensing requirements may still apply.

Direct route to membership

This provides a direct route to membership for eligible members. Local practising rights are not automatically conferred and additional local requirements may apply.

Memorandum of understanding (MoU)

This provides a framework for co-operation, information sharing, recognition discussions, or pathways between organisations. It does not automatically confer practising rights or recognition unless explicitly stated.

Mutual Recognition Agreement (MRA)

A formal agreement between 2 or more parties (usually regulatory bodies) which aims to facilitate mobility of professionals through agreed mutual recognition, registration or membership processes. Subject to agreed criteria and local requirements.

Mutual Recognition of Professional Qualifications (MRPQ)

This provides reciprocal recognition of professional qualifications between participating bodies, subject to any specified eligibility criteria and local requirements.

Pathway to membership/study route

This provides a route to body membership through examinations, additional study, experience requirements or other prescribed criteria. Local practising rights are not automatically conferred.

Reciprocal Membership Agreement

This provides a reciprocal membership route for eligible members. Local practising rights are not automatically conferred and local licensing requirements may still apply.

Recognition / practice route

This provides a route to recognition for practice in the overseas jurisdiction, subject to local conditions.

Regulatory co-operation

This provides a regulatory co-operation framework. Local practising rights are not automatically conferred.
